« Nos quartiers, nos voix » – Dialogue e: “Our Neighbourhoods, Our Voices” – Community workers come together in dialogue on the rise in violent crime among youth
La Converse a organisé une rencontre ave: La Converse hosted a meeting with community workers who work with young people, to better understand the issues affecting them.
De gauche à droite, rangée du haut: Andr: From left to right, top row: Andrew Joseph, Abdellah Azzouz and Salim El Asri. Bottom row: Mohamed Mimoun, Myriam Coppry and Riguerre Antoine. Photo: Aude Simon
Il y a quelques semaines, des dizaines d: A few weeks ago, dozens of parents of teenagers gathered in Saint-Léonard, right next to the pond in Parc Wilfrid-Bastien. The gathering was meant as a response to families’ worries about the recruitment of young people by street gang members. The older gang members are allegedly using their influence to lure their juniors in, promising easy money in exchange for criminal activity.
Un peu plus tard le même jour, des inter: A little later that same day, community workers from all corners of the island of Montréal came to the La Converse offices. Unhappy with the way the problem described above is portrayed in traditional media, they put their heads together and concluded that there was a lack of communication among the community players who surround young people. They also condemn the way certain media outlets treat the phenomenon, which creates a climate of division and rivalry among racialized youth instead of promoting collaboration and solidarity.
C’est pour cela que, le 18 octobre derni: That is why, on October 18, La Converse hosted a meeting with community workers who work with young people, and with parents as well, to better understand the issues that hit them hardest as we witness a resurgence of violent crime among minors.
Les intervenants sont venus vers nous, e: The community workers came to us, and that, in my opinion, is what does the greatest service to everyone affected by the rise in crime. Of course, this report deals with a sensitive subject – and a sensitive subject means limits and a need for delicacy. Moderating this dialogue, which took the form of a panel, was enriching and relevant. Writing this report, however, was not as smooth, because writing about a subject that negatively affects entire families is never easy.
Il faut garder en tête que, lorsqu’on ut: We have to keep in mind that when we use words like “young offender” or “delinquent,” some people hear “criminal.” We have to try to use vocabulary that doesn’t further marginalize the people concerned – victims and perpetrators alike, who, on both sides, are minors. In short, terminology and the way a phenomenon is presented always change the picture, but when we write about a subject tied to young people who have lost their lives violently, we have to be doubly careful.
Je vous laisse donc suivre ce dialogue q: So I’ll let you follow this dialogue, which for many put a bandage on a painful wound… and which for others offered a chance to reflect on ideas often forgotten in public discourse.
Bonne lecture et à bientôt !: Happy reading, and see you soon!
<strong>Lorsque des intervenants ont cog: When community workers knocked on La Converse’s door a few weeks ago, we quickly understood the urgency that drove them to come to us. “We have to find a solution, we have to create a dialogue,” they told us, almost in unison. The troubling subject? Violence that is taking up more and more space in the lives of a number of teenagers in Montréal. Violence that is encouraged by gangs and that affects racialized communities more than others.
Par une chaude soirée d’automne, Andrew: On a warm autumn evening, Andrew Joseph, Salim El Asri, Myriam Coppry, Riguerre Antoine, Abdellah Azzouz and Mohamed Mimoun, all youth workers, along with parents, passed the microphone around in our offices. For the length of a dialogue, they spoke to us and tried to explain the different facets of the gun violence that is claiming more and more young people.
Au cours des dernières années, si on vit: If you’ve lived in Montréal or its surroundings in recent years, it’s hard to have missed a troubling phenomenon: young people falling victim to violence that is increasingly rampant in the streets of the metropolis.
<strong><em>7 février 2021. </em></stron: February 7, 2021. It’s hard to forget Meriem Boundaoui, 15, killed by a stray bullet while she was in a vehicle in broad daylight in the Saint-Léonard borough.
<strong><em>14 novembre 2021.</em></stro: November 14, 2021. A few months later, Thomas Trudel dies at 16, murdered as he was walking home in Saint-Michel.
<strong><em>13 janvier 2022.</em></stron: January 13, 2022. Late in the evening, Amir Benayad, 17, is shot dead in a park in the Plateau-Mont-Royal.
<strong><em>28 mars 2024. </em></strong>: March 28, 2024. Mehdi Moussaoui, 14, and Marley St-Surin, 16, die of their injuries following a car crash in the early morning, after they had shot at passersby.
<strong><em>17 septembre 2024. </em></st: September 17, 2024. Mohamed-Yanis Seghouani, a 14-year-old from Montréal, is found dead near a hideout of an outlaw motorcycle gang in Beauce. He was armed.
Ce ne sont là qu’un petit nombre des diz: These are only a small number of the dozens of young people who have lost their lives in a context of gun violence in Montréal in recent years. What happened to these young people? And in what context did such a worrying environment take hold – especially among teenagers and young adults from diverse backgrounds? Experts and community workers discuss.
« C’est complexe », répond <strong>Andre: “It’s complex,” answers Andrew Joseph. The community worker with Équipe RDP, a nonprofit created in 1990 in Rivière-des-Prairies to counter juvenile delinquency, works with young people in his neighbourhood and therefore knows well what they go through every day. He also coaches sports teams made up of high school students in Montréal-Nord. In his view, young people are under enormous pressure, both personally and socially. “Teenagers live lives that are different from ours. They’re a whole new generation facing different challenges,” he says.
Pour comprendre les jeunes, il faut jete: To understand young people, you have to look at the society they’re growing up in, the community worker continues. “Today, they survive more than they spend time living,” he goes on. “What we dangle in front of [them] is often very different from what they experience. For example, growing up, they learn that as adults they’ll find work and won’t have any problems if they follow the rules. Then, when they get to 16, 17, 18, nobody hires them, and they often feel excluded,” he sums up. He adds that this is often a problem faced by racialized youth.
« À partir de ce moment-là, c’est très f: “From that moment on, it’s very easy for a young person to turn to something else. Unconsciously, they feel they can’t fit in, by finding a job, for example. So they start looking at how to get certain things, how to fill their free time; and that’s where they become vulnerable and easily influenced,” he adds in one breath. Easy money then becomes an option for some, who are drawn in by the lure of profit.
<strong>Abdellah Azzouz</strong>, interv: Abdellah Azzouz, a community worker at the Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel, shares that view. He wants to qualify some of what his colleague from Rivière-des-Prairies said, however: “A lot is going on with young people. We can try to explain where the negative comes from, as Andrew did, but we can also see that there’s positive and try to explain it so it spreads,” he says in an optimistic tone.
D’origine algérienne et âgé de 25 ans, c: Of Algerian origin and 25 years old, Azzouz, who goes by his last name, is well known to young people in his neighbourhood, most of whom are North African. He shares some of the feelings teenagers have, like frustration, anger and exclusion, having himself grown up in a stigmatized neighbourhood. But he wants to bet on teenagers, because he recognizes their potential. “We get to see young people who change and become different people. Young people who come up with ideas and who want the authorities to listen to them instead of talking about them,” he says.
Les jeunes qui commettent des crimes ne: Young people who commit crimes don’t all do it for the same reason, he points out. “In the short term, some do it for money. Yet most don’t do it for money, but to be recognized by the people around them and to boost the sense of belonging they may not have elsewhere,” he analyzes.
<strong>Myriam Coppry</strong> est coach: Myriam Coppry is a coach for parents from diverse backgrounds. For several years, she has worked with parents who, often left to fend for themselves, end up deeply discouraged when they have to deal with the Direction de la protection de la jeunesse (DPJ).
« S’il y a une chose que je dénonce, c’e: “If there’s one thing I condemn, it’s that very little room, or none at all, is left for parents when we talk about intervening with young people,” she is quick to say. She doesn’t understand how isolating parents could help their children. What she does know is that it makes the situation worse. “We’re dealing with parents abandoned by the system, who don’t know what to do to remedy the situation, and who sometimes don’t even know what the situation is!” she exclaims.
Pour la coach, il est inadmissible que d: For the coach, it is unacceptable that parents are not informed of the intervention plans prepared for their children. “You can’t solve a problem if you break the bond. You always have to keep the bond – between parents and children, between parents and the system,” she says, pushing her glasses back up her nose.
« Depuis quelques mois, j’entends dire p: “For the past few months, I’ve been hearing everywhere: ‘Where are the parents? How could they not know their kids were mixed up in crime? It’s up to parents to take good care of their kids so this doesn’t happen again.’” Blaming parents like this only adds fuel to the fire, she believes. “You can’t blame [them] once the damage is done and push them aside when it’s time to find a solution. It’s hypocrisy,” she says firmly. “We have to learn to empower parents without blaming them.”
C’est au tour de <strong>Mohamed Mimoun<: It is now Mohamed Mimoun’s turn to speak. The coordinator of the Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel is no stranger to speaking up: in Montréal, he is a true pillar, for young people and for North African parents alike who are confronted with this youth violence.
« La sécurité, c’est un enjeu qui concer: “Safety is an issue that concerns everyone. But when we talk about fighting violence, what worries me is how that safety becomes a tool in the hands of some,” he begins. Even though he speaks softly, the father has a certain seriousness in his voice that commands respect. “Right now, parents are afraid to ask for help for their kids because they fear their children will be taken away,” he says, indignant.
Certains parents avec qui il travaille s: Some of the parents he works with distrust the police and institutions in general, he says. “It may be a detail to some, but for others, it can be the reason a child is lost,” he says bitterly.
<strong>Riguerre Antoine</strong> prend: Riguerre Antoine finally takes the floor. A street outreach worker in Rivière-des-Prairies since 1997, he is considered a pioneer of youth intervention in his neighbourhood. “When we accept the term ‘marginalized,’ it means we accept living on the margins of society. I refuse that, and I think our young people should accept it even less, especially when we know that many of them were born and raised in Montréal,” he declares forcefully.
Contrairement à M. Mimoun, qui a pris la: Unlike Mr. Mimoun, who spoke just before him, Mr. Antoine’s voice rumbles through the La Converse studios. And just as some of the young people in the audience were starting to get distracted as the speakers went on, it’s as if Riguerre refocused their attention. “What’s happening in Montréal isn’t only happening here. There are young people committing crimes all over the world since the dawn of time,” he explains. “We shouldn’t think that because we come from Montréal, belong to a racialized community and are overrepresented in the news briefs, it’s a life sentence,” he says.
« Je veux rappeler aux jeunes qu’ils son: “I want to remind young people that they’re at home here. We mustn’t think we don’t belong in this society, even if sometimes it’s easy to believe that,” he continues. “Our young people must not live on the margins; they are an integral part of society.” He adds, raising his shoulders: “There may be no magic solution, but there is hope and a better future, that’s for sure.”
Avant même que quelqu’un d’autre ne pren: Before anyone else can speak, a wave of applause echoes through the room. Community workers, young people, parents and the audience seem to welcome the words of the Équipe RDP pioneer with joy. “The magic solution doesn’t exist,” Salim El Asri picks up, as the last of the applause can be heard, “but there are ways to better prevent tragedies.”
Coordonnateur du travail de rue et de la: The coordinator of street outreach and prevention at Prévention Pointe-de-l’Île, an organization in the east end of the city, he revisits just about all the themes his fellow speakers raised over the past hour. “Young people and families not understanding the system, and an enormous gap between society and young people: that’s what worries our youth,” he says. “I’m not pulling this out of thin air; they’re the ones telling us,” he assures.
Les jeunes ne sont pas assez écoutés, va: Young people are not listened to, valued or taken into consideration enough: that is the root of the problem, he believes. “Exclusion, from all sides, isolates young people, and the message we send them is that they have no place here. Let’s help them and be there for them,” he says with a hint of emotion in his voice.
Fort de ses 13 ans d’expérience en inter: With 13 years of experience in outreach, Salim has seen it all. The Pointe-aux-Trembles worker remains absolutely certain of one thing, though: “We love young people, and they need to know it. We think they know it through what we do, but we have to tell them clearly,” he says passionately.
La soirée tire à sa fin. La fatigue comm: The evening is drawing to a close. Fatigue is starting to show among the young people, who have been there since the start of the discussion. While our guests each raised different aspects of the resurgence of violent crime among teenagers, they are unanimous on one point: even though the motivations that push young people toward delinquency are many, “the consequences are the same,” Salim reminds us. And that is what we must keep in mind, he adds.
